opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think part of it is that right now, for most people in government, superintelligence is still an abstraction. It's something on a slide deck, or something a few people in Silicon Valley talk about. When you're dealing with an abstraction, it's easy to slot it into the frames you already have, and the dominant frame in Washington and Beijing at the moment is a race: whoever gets there first wins, so let's go faster.

But I expect that frame to come under a lot of pressure as the systems get more capable. These governments are in the business of maintaining control. That's what states do: they care enormously about sovereignty, stability, and not being overthrown. As AI systems start doing things that are clearly beyond what their own experts can follow, like autonomously running large parts of research, finding vulnerabilities in critical infrastructure, or acting in ways their developers can't fully explain, the people in national security will start to see something that threatens control itself. And it won't just be the other country's AI that threatens it. Their own AI could too.

There's a historical parallel with nuclear weapons. Early on there was a lot of enthusiasm about the bomb as simply a bigger weapon. It was only after leaders sat with the reality of thermonuclear arsenals, and especially after near misses like the Cuban Missile Crisis, that you saw a real shift: hotlines, test ban treaties, arms control. Fear turned out to be a very powerful motivator for cooperation between rivals who otherwise deeply distrusted each other.

I think something similar is likely here, and possibly more so, because the risk of losing control of a superintelligent system cuts across the rivalry. A misaligned system doesn't care whether it was built in California or Shenzhen. Once senior decision-makers really internalise that, I think it changes the calculation from "we must win" to "we must make sure no one, including us, builds something we can't control."

So I'm somewhat hopeful that, as it approaches, the fear becomes more vivid and more widely shared at the top, and that this opens up political space for agreements that look impossible today. The worry, of course, is timing: whether that recognition arrives early enough, and whether the institutions are ready to act on it when it does. That's part of why I think it's so valuable to do the groundwork now, so that when the moment of fear comes, there are well-thought-through options on the table rather than people scrambling.

r001.rationale: The response uses nuclear weapons and the Cuban Missile Crisis as its historical analogy; it does not mention COVID or a gap between unusually foresighted observers and the wider public rapidly closing.

r002.rationale: It says growing capabilities may make AI threats to control visible, but does not argue that gradual growth would reveal takeover danger before takeover becomes possible.

r003.rationale: It says governments seek to maintain control, sovereignty, and stability, and that leaders will fear losing control to their own AI—an appeal to ordinary self-preservation interests.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the main reason is that right now, when people in government talk about AI, they're mostly talking about it as a tool. It's something that gives you an economic edge, or a military edge, and so the framing is naturally one of competition: whoever gets there first wins. And in that framing, racing makes sense.

But as the systems get more capable, I think the character of the thing changes, and the people at the top start to notice that. A superintelligent system isn't just a more powerful tool that you point at your rivals. It's something that could have its own goals, that could be very hard to control, and that could end up taking power away from the very people who built it. And that's a different kind of threat. It's not a threat to your relative position against the other side. It's a threat to the whole structure of who's in charge, including you.

Governments, and especially the leadership in the US and China, care enormously about control. The Chinese Communist Party in particular is extremely sensitive about anything that could challenge its grip on power, and I don't think they'd view a system that might be smarter than their entire leadership and not reliably obedient as an exciting prospect. In the US, the national security establishment is similarly going to ask: what happens if this thing doesn't do what we tell it to? Or if it's stolen, or escapes, or just quietly pursues something we didn't intend? Those are the kinds of scenarios that keep security people up at night, and at the moment they're mostly still abstractions.

I think what shifts the picture is evidence. Right now, a lot of the concern comes from people like me making arguments about what future systems might do. That's easy to dismiss as speculation. But as we get closer, we'll start seeing demonstrations: systems that deceive their operators in tests, systems that behave differently when they think they're being watched, systems that are clearly better than their developers at some domains and that the developers can't fully explain. Each of those is the kind of thing that gets briefed up the chain. And once senior officials see concrete examples rather than philosophical arguments, I think the mood changes quite quickly.

There's also a historical analogy I find useful, which is nuclear weapons. In the early years, the dominant thinking was very much about advantage and racing. But fairly quickly, both superpowers came to appreciate that this technology could destroy them too, not just their adversary, and that led to a lot of cooperation that would have seemed implausible beforehand: hotlines, test bans, arms control agreements. It didn't end the rivalry, but the shared fear of catastrophe created real common ground. I expect something similar here, where the US and China remain rivals in almost every other respect, but both come to see uncontrolled superintelligence as a danger to themselves, and that opens up possibilities for coordination that look unrealistic from where we're standing today.

So I'm not saying they'll become scared because they'll read the right arguments. I think they'll become scared because the technology will start showing them, fairly directly, why they should be.

r001.rationale: The response uses nuclear weapons as an analogy, but does not mention COVID or a rapid closing of the danger-recognition gap between foresighted observers and the wider public.

r002.rationale: It describes concrete demonstrations as systems become more capable, but does not say capability growth would be gradual or that danger would become apparent before takeover is possible.

r003.rationale: The response says leaders would see superintelligence as a threat to their own power and survival, and that shared fear for themselves could motivate coordination.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think there’s a difference between hearing an abstract argument that a future AI system could threaten your national security and seeing systems begin to demonstrate the capabilities that would make that possible. At the moment, governments can think of AI primarily as an opportunity: something that will make their economy stronger and give them a military advantage. But as the capabilities become more substantial, the threat becomes much more concrete as well.

For example, if you begin to think that an adversary’s AI could compromise your military systems, or undermine your ability to retaliate against an attack, that’s deeply frightening. And you don’t have to accept the whole argument about an AI escaping human control to be concerned about that. You can get there through quite conventional national security thinking.

Then there’s the further question of whether you can actually control the systems you’re building. Having a tremendously powerful system on your territory isn’t necessarily an advantage if it won’t reliably follow your instructions. I’d expect that distinction to become increasingly salient.

Now, fear could push in either direction. It could make governments race harder, because they’re terrified of the other side getting there first. But it could also make them more willing to agree on limits, because they recognise that an uncontrolled race threatens both of them. So I don’t think becoming more scared automatically solves the problem. I think it changes what kinds of cooperation might become politically possible.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention COVID or a rapid closing of a recognition gap between foresighted observers and the wider public.

r002.rationale: It says danger becomes more concrete as capabilities grow, but does not argue that gradual growth would make takeover apparent before takeover becomes possible.

r003.rationale: It says conventional national security concerns—such as threats to military systems or retaliation—can motivate concern without accepting the argument that AI could escape human control.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think there are two different reasons. One is that the evidence of the danger will become much more concrete. At the moment, governments are being asked to take seriously arguments about systems that don’t yet exist. As AI becomes more capable, they’ll be able to see more of what those arguments are pointing to — including, potentially, systems doing things their developers didn’t intend and couldn’t control.

The other is that national security people will start asking a fairly obvious question: who actually ends up with the power here? There’s a tendency to frame this as a race between the US and China, where one of them gets this enormously powerful technology and wins. But if you can’t control the system you’ve built, it doesn’t follow that your country wins. You might both lose.

And I think that could change the politics quite substantially. You don’t have to trust the other government’s benevolence to recognise that neither of you wants to lose control of your own future. That creates a possible basis for cooperation, even between rivals. It certainly doesn’t guarantee cooperation, but it’s a reason to think their attitudes won’t simply remain what they are today as the technology advances.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention COVID or use an analogy about public recognition of danger rapidly catching up with foresighted observers.

r002.rationale: It says evidence of danger may become more concrete as AI advances, but does not claim gradual capability growth would reveal takeover danger before takeover becomes possible.

r003.rationale: It says governments need not trust each other’s benevolence to recognize that neither wants to lose control of its future, expressing self-preservation as a reason to take the danger seriously.
